svg.title: Imperative vs. declarative migrations
svg.desc: The same change described two ways: add an email column to the customers table, which already has three rows: Ana Lopez, Ben Park, and Cai Wu. Imperative (versioned): you plan the steps yourself and write them in a new migration file, 20250203140000_add_email_to_customers, containing ALTER TABLE customers ADD COLUMN email TEXT. The file is reviewed in source control, and the tool runs every file the database has not run yet, in timestamp order, exactly as written. Declarative (state-based), with Supabase's declarative schemas: you edit supabase/schemas/customers.sql so that CREATE TABLE customers lists id, name, and email. The Supabase CLI compares the schema files with the schema your existing migrations produce, finds that email exists only in the schema files, and writes the difference to a new migration file in supabase/migrations/: alter table public.customers add column email text. You review the generated file, then push it with supabase db push, as usual. Both end the same way: customers gains an email column, NULL for the three existing customers, and every existing row is kept. The difference is what you write and who plans the steps.
svg.text: Imperative vs. declarative: who plans the migration?
Same change, same result. Imperative migrations spell out how to get there.
A declarative schema says where to end up, and the Supabase CLI writes the steps.
